## Research Proposals: Fixes Most of You Still Need to Make

- **Framing:** write three to five one-sentence points that name the platform, the accounts, and the dates
- **Theory:** write numbered points that say what the theory leads you to expect in your own material
- **Literature:** group the studies by theme and say what they show together, not one study at a time
- **Gap:** name the two or three closest studies, say what each did not do, and state the question that is still open
- **Hypotheses:** state that two things you record are associated ("is associated with"); never write "will" or "leads to"

::: {.notes}
Each student's own version of these points, with examples from their own topic, is in their written feedback.
:::

## Research Proposals: Fixes for Your Coding Plan

- **What you code:** name the unit you code (for example, one post or one comment) and the fixed categories each item can receive
- **Recode check:** code about 10 percent of your items again, 48 or more hours later, with your first codes hidden; rewrite the rule behind any code that changed
- **Comparison:** for each research question, say what you will compare, and match it to the level of measurement of each variable

::: {.notes}
Each student's own version of these points, with examples from their own topic, is in their written feedback.
:::

## Research Proposals: Fixes for Your Sample and Claims

- **Sample:** write selection rules someone else could follow to collect the same set, rather than picking items because they fit
- **Sample size:** choose a number of items you can finish coding before Describing Data on November 16
- **Claims:** claim only what your coded material can show; make no claims about causes and no predictions

::: {.notes}
Each student's own version of these points, with examples from their own topic, is in their written feedback.
:::

    - The level you choose decides which statistical tests you may run in November
    - By November there is no time to recode your sample at a different level
- **The second topic is the codebook**
    - The assignments in the second half of this course all build on your codebook
- **Due Monday, October 19, 11:59 PM:** Definitions Practice

## The Four Levels of Measurement (NOIR)

- **Every variable you measure has a level of measurement**
    - The level decides which statistics you may use on it later
- **NOIR names the four levels: nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio**
- **The `stream_log` columns give an example of each level**
    - The columns are channel, title, game, viewers, and date

The data does not fix the level. The level depends on how you decide to measure the variable.

## Nominal

- **Nominal variables are categories with no built-in order**
    - `game`: Fortnite, Just Chatting, Art, Hearthstone
    - You cannot add, subtract, or rank the categories
- **`channel` is nominal, and so is `title` kept as its original text**
- **You can count each category and report the most common one**

You cannot average a nominal variable: there is no average of Fortnite and Art.

## Ordinal

- **Ordinal variables are ordered categories with unequal distances between them**
    - Example: group titles by length into short, medium, and long
    - A long title ranks above a short one
- **The distances between categories are not guaranteed to be equal**
    - The step from short to medium may differ in size from the step from medium to long
- You can rank cases and report the **median**, but a mean is not meaningful

## Interval

- **Interval variables have equal distances and a zero point set by convention**
    - Example: the date and time each message was posted
    - One minute is the same length anywhere in the column
- **The zero point, 1970, is a convention; it does not mean "no time"**
    - `date` stores each time as milliseconds counted from 1970
- Ratios are meaningless: a message posted at 2:00 was not posted twice as late as one posted at 1:00

## Ratio

- **Ratio variables have equal distances and a true zero**
    - `viewers` is ratio: zero means nobody is watching
    - So 28,000 viewers is twice the audience of 14,000 viewers
- **Elapsed time, such as hours since the stream started, is ratio**
    - Subtracting one timestamp from another gives a duration, which is ratio
- **You may add, subtract, multiply, and divide ratio values**
- Most counts are ratio, such as viewers, characters, and messages

## One Column Can Be Measured at Three Levels

The `title` column of `stream_log`, measured three ways:

- **Kept as the original text:** nominal
- **Counted in characters:** ratio, because a title can have zero characters
- **Grouped into short, medium, and long:** ordinal

The level depends on how you choose to measure the column.

## Exercise: Name the Level of Each Variable

For each variable, name its level of measurement and the feature that shows it: whether the
values are ordered, whether the distances are equal, and whether zero means none.

1. Whether a comment contains a question: yes or no
2. A product review's star rating, one to five
3. The date and time a post was published
4. The number of words in a headline
5. Minutes since the stream began

The same three checks work for data from any platform.

## Which Statistics Each Level Allows

| Level | Summarize it with | Test it with |
|---|---|---|
| Nominal | Counts and the most common value | Chi-square test of association |
| Ordinal | The median and the ranks | Rank-based tests |
| Interval | The mean and standard deviation | t-test, ANOVA, and correlation |
| Ratio | Everything above, plus ratios between values | The interval tests; you may also say one value is twice another |

Definitions Practice asks for one sentence per variable that names its level and says which
statistics it allows and which it rules out.

## Measuring at a Lower Level Than Needed Limits Your Tests

- **Recording a variable as nominal when ratio was possible removes the tests that need ratio data**
    - That limit is set before you code a single item
- **The problem is usually not visible while you are coding**
    - It appears in November, when a test you planned is not allowed
    - By then you have already spent many hours coding

## Two Kinds of Variable: Ready-Made and Coded

- **Some variables arrive ready-made in the data**
    - `viewers` is a number, `game` is a category
    - Your only task is to identify the level
- **Other variables exist only after a person codes them**
    - Message target (who a chat message is addressed to) is not a column in `chat_log`
    - It exists only after a coder reads each message and assigns a category

Coders assign categories consistently only when they follow written instructions, and the
codebook is those instructions.

## Exercise: Match Each Definition to Its Failure

[Recap from Week 7]{.eyebrow}

Each operational definition below fails in one of the four ways listed at the bottom. Name
the failure for each.

1. **Community strength** in a subreddit: posts per day
2. **Sincerity** of a review: coded sincere when the writer means it
3. **Article quality**: how many times it was shared
4. **Engagement** with a video: the comment count, and nothing else

The four failures: conflating concepts, the unjustified proxy, oversimplification, and the
unmeasurable definition.

## Reliability Means Consistency

- **A reliable measure gives the same result under the same conditions**
    - A bathroom scale that reads 150, then 162, then 147 for the same person is useless
- **In content analysis, reliability means coders apply the codebook consistently**
    - **Intercoder:** two coders code the same messages independently
    - **Intracoder, or stability:** one coder codes the same messages twice
- **Kappa and alpha measure agreement after removing the agreement expected by chance**

## Validity Means Accuracy

- **A valid measure captures the concept it claims to measure**
- **Face validity:** the measure looks like a reasonable way to measure the concept
- **Content validity:** the measure covers every part of the concept
- **Construct validity:** the measure relates to other variables the way theory says it should

You support validity with a written argument; no statistic calculates it.

## Reliability and Validity Are Independent

- **Reliable but not valid:** a scale that always reads ten pounds too light
    - It gives the same reading every time, and the reading is wrong every time
- **Valid but not reliable:** a scale that is correct on average
    - Its readings vary so much that no single reading can be trusted

A measure must be reliable before it can be valid, but reliability alone does not make it
valid. You establish reliability first, because a clear codebook is what produces it.

## Writing the Validity Sentence

- **Definitions Practice asks for one validity sentence per variable**
    - It says what would make you doubt the variable measures your concept
- **Name another explanation for what your number could mean**
    - Message length as engagement: a long pasted block can come from a disengaged sender
    - Share count as quality: outrage articles get shared as often as good ones
- **Write the doubt, not a reassurance**
    - "It measures what I say it does" states no doubt, so it does not count

A good validity sentence describes a case where the number is recorded correctly but does not
reflect the concept.

## Discussion: Reliability When You Are the Only Coder {.discuss}

[Lombard et al. (2002)]{.eyebrow}

> "It is widely acknowledged that intercoder reliability is a critical component of content
> analysis and (although it does not ensure validity) when it is not established, the data
> and interpretations of the data can never be considered valid."
>
> Lombard et al. (2002, p. 589)

Your study has one coder, so intercoder reliability cannot be established. Discuss two questions:

1. Is the quote a standard to work toward, or a verdict that your data cannot be valid? Give a reason.
2. What can you honestly claim from one coder's data? Name one claim you can make and one you cannot.

## The Risk When the Researcher Is the Coder

> "Coding must be done independently and without consultation or guidance. If possible, the
> researcher should not be a coder."
>
> Lombard et al. (2002, p. 601)

- **In your study you are both researcher and coder**
    - Question: what specific risk does that create, and what would catch it? A good answer names one way your expectations could change a code and one check that would reveal it
- **A codebook pilot of about 30 units is the usual rule of thumb** (Lombard et al., 2002)
- **The reliability sample you report needs at least 50 units or 10 percent of the sample, and rarely more than 300** (Lombard et al., 2002)

## The Standard Two-Coder Protocol, Steps 1 and 2

When a study has two coders, the standard reliability protocol has four steps, done in this
order. Your second-coder counterfactual describes this protocol.

1. The second coder receives the **codebook alone**, with no explanation from you, and codes a
   training set of 20 to 30 units independently.
2. The two coders **compare and discuss every disagreement**. No production data is coded
   at this stage.

In step 1 you may not explain what you meant; the codebook must work on its own.

## The Standard Two-Coder Protocol, Steps 3 and 4

3. The **codebook is revised**, adding a decision rule for every disagreement.
4. The second coder codes a **fresh reliability sample**, separate from the training set.
   That agreement is the kappa you report.

- **Do not report the agreement from the training set**
    - It is inflated, because the coders discussed those same units in step 2
- **Report more than one agreement statistic** (Lombard et al., 2002)

## Percent Agreement Alone Is Not Enough

- **Do not report percent agreement by itself**
    - Two coders guessing on a yes-or-no variable agree half the time
    - Kappa and alpha subtract the agreement expected by chance

## Which Reliability Statistic to Report

- **One approach: report one standard measure, alpha** (Hayes & Krippendorff, 2007)
    - Alpha works with any number of coders, any level of measurement, and missing codes
- **Another approach: report two or more statistics, with a decision rule** (Lombard et al., 2002)
    - Accept when a conservative statistic reaches a moderate value or a liberal one reaches a high value
- Your protocol names the statistic you will report and explains why you chose it

## Reliability Thresholds

- **State your threshold, with its source, before you compute the statistic**
    - Kappa of 0.70 or higher is the course floor (Landis & Koch, 1977)
    - 0.90 nearly always acceptable, 0.80 in most situations, 0.70 in some exploratory studies (Lombard et al., 2002)
    - Alpha of 0.80, or 0.667 for tentative conclusions (Krippendorff, 2018)
- **If the result is below your threshold, revise the codebook; a caveat is not enough**

Two passes that agree on 40 of 50 units have 80 percent agreement. That is not kappa, so
compute kappa before comparing the result with the 0.70 floor.

## Reliability Sample Size and Computing Kappa

- **The reliability sample needs at least 50 coded units**
    - If some categories are rare, 100 or more units are preferred
- **`v2v::reliability()` computes kappa and labels its strength, such as "substantial"**

## The One-Coder Protocol You Will Run

You have no second coder, so you report **stability** (intracoder reliability), and your
protocol uses that word.

1. **Re-code at least 10 percent** of your coded items, **48 hours or more** later, with your
   first codes **hidden**
2. Draw that sample **fresh**, at random from items you did not use to build or revise the codebook
3. **Report the statistic even if it is lower than you hoped**, with the revision rule you would apply
4. Name **three safeguards** against your coding drifting over time, and write the second-coder counterfactual

## Stability Compared with Two-Coder Agreement

In this course, 10 percent is enough to practice; published studies re-code 10 to 20 percent.

Stability is weaker evidence than agreement between two coders. Following the four steps of
the one-coder protocol makes your stability report honest.

::: {.notes}
In this course about 10 percent is enough to practice the mechanics; a study meant for publication re-codes 10 to 20 percent of its items. The reported reliability sample is no fewer than 50 units or 10 percent of the full sample (Lombard, Snyder-Duch, & Bracken, 2002).
:::

## If Your Reliability Falls Below the Threshold

- **Write your revision rule now, before you see the number**
    - The rule says which categories you will revise and how
- **Use the list of items your two passes coded differently**
    - For each one, rewrite the codebook rule that failed to decide it
    - Do not settle a disagreement by re-reading your first codes and going with your feeling
- **Keep a record so the codebook does not drift toward your habits**
    - Log every change with its date and reason
    - Re-code the affected items under the new version
- **Report the first number anyway**, and explain what it showed you about the codebook

## Five Safeguards: Use at Least Three

Your protocol names at least three of these that you actually use, and describes what you do
for each.

1. **Inclusion and exclusion rules** for every category, written before coding begins
2. **Prototypical examples**, two or three per category, drawn from your corpus
3. **A frozen codebook**, with every later change logged by date and reason
4. **An ambiguous-case memo**, decided by the written rule rather than by feel
5. **A fixed coding order**, with source details such as the account name hidden wherever possible

## The Second-Coder Counterfactual

Write one paragraph describing how you would have measured reliability with a second coder.
It covers four points.

1. **How many items** you would have double-coded
2. **Which statistic** you would have reported
3. **How you would have trained** the second coder and settled disagreements
4. **Which finding is most at risk** if the second coder had disagreed with you

Points 1 to 3 come from the standard two-coder protocol earlier in this deck. Point 4 asks
you to judge which of your own findings depends most on your coding.

## Why a Reliability Protocol Is Required

> "Conclusions from such data can be trusted only after demonstrating their reliability."
>
> Hayes and Krippendorff (2007, p. 77)

- **Either protocol, two-coder or one-coder, provides the demonstration this quote requires**
- **Every later analysis depends on the codes being reliable**
- A finding from a codebook whose reliability was never tested has no support

## The Codebook Is Your Measuring Instrument

- **The codebook is not paperwork written to satisfy a requirement**
- **If coding were a computer program, the codebook would be its source code**
    - It specifies every step and every if-then decision
    - Run on the same input twice, it gives the same output
- The codebook is the core of a content analysis (Neuendorf, 2017)

## Five Parts of a Codebook

1. **Unit of analysis:** exactly what one coded case is
2. **Variables and categories:** the conceptual and operational definition of each variable, and every value it can take
3. **Decision rules:** what to do when a case does not fit one category cleanly
4. **Examples:** two or three prototypes per category, from your own material
5. **Special cases:** complications that keep recurring; this section starts short and grows as you code

## Categories Must Be Exhaustive and Mutually Exclusive

- **Exhaustive:** every case fits some category
    - A catch-all category, such as "unclassifiable," guarantees this
- **Mutually exclusive:** every case fits exactly one category
    - If categories overlap, coders keep disagreeing on the same cases, and reliability drops
- **To fix overlap, sharpen the definitions or add a precedence rule that says which category wins**

If more than 10 percent of cases land in the catch-all, the categories are incomplete and need
revision.

## Example Codebook: Unit and Message Target

> **Unit of analysis.** A single chat message, defined as one row of `chat_log`: one
> sender, one message string, one timestamp. Each message is coded independently of those
> around it, except where a decision rule says otherwise.

> **Variable 1: message target.** Categories: directed at streamer, directed at another
> viewer, broadcast to the room, unclassifiable. Level: nominal.

## Example Codebook: Message Length and Emotes

> **Variable 2: message length.** Conceptual: the verbal extent of the message.
> Operational: the count of characters, including spaces and emote tokens. Counted, not
> judged by a coder. Level: ratio.

> **Variable 3: contains emote.** Operational: yes if the message contains at least one
> token from the project's emote list. Level: nominal.

Message length and contains emote are manifest: anyone can count them. Message target is
latent: a coder must interpret it. The example mixes both kinds on purpose.

## The Example Codebook's Five Decision Rules

1. **Precedence:** a message that directly addresses someone is coded as directed at them, even if it also plays to the room
2. **Emote-only messages:** coded broadcast to the room, unless the message includes an @-mention
3. **Copypasta** (a block of text many viewers paste): coded by its content, like any other message
4. **Messages not in English:** code the target only when the message's structure, such as an @-mention, shows it
5. **Bot accounts:** coded unclassifiable and flagged for possible exclusion

## Exercise: Sort Rules from Intentions

A rule is an instruction a coder can apply without asking you. An intention is a wish that
leaves the decision to the coder. Label each item below a rule or an intention.

1. Be careful with sarcasm
2. A message made only of emotes is coded broadcast to the room
3. Use judgment on posts in a language you do not read
4. A reply that quotes an earlier comment is coded directed at another viewer

Definitions Practice asks for two decision rules per variable. An intention written in place of
a rule earns no credit.

Due Monday, October 19, 11:59 PM. Define at least four variables, and give each one all six
elements, written the way they will appear in your codebook.

1. **Conceptual definition**, with a citation to where the construct comes from
    - If you invented the construct, add a sentence explaining why it is needed
2. **Operational definition:** the steps a coder performs to assign a value, not the conceptual definition reworded
3. **Level of measurement**, with one sentence on which statistics it allows and which it rules out

## Definitions Practice: The Six Required Elements, 4 to 6

4. **Coded values:** every value, what each means, and a catch-all category
5. **Two decision rules for edge cases**, each written as a rule a coder can apply
6. **One validity sentence:** what would make you doubt the variable measures your concept
